0.title: Caring for Souls with the Word of God
0.overview:
Biblical counseling begins with a conviction: that the Word of God and the Spirit of God are sufficient to address the deepest struggles of the human soul. This is not a claim that the Bible is a medical textbook or that it addresses every technical question in psychiatry — it is a claim that the Scriptures contain everything necessary for life and godliness (2 Pet 1:3), and that the God who made the human heart is the only one who fully understands it and can truly heal it.

The modern biblical counseling movement grew largely as a response to the church's capitulation to secular psychology in the mid-twentieth century. Jay Adams, in his landmark Competent to Counsel (1970), argued that pastors had surrendered the cure of souls — the ancient task of the church — to secular therapists who operated with fundamentally different (and often antithetical) assumptions about human nature, sin, and the good life. Adams's nouthetic (from the Greek noutheteo — to admonish, instruct, counsel) approach recovered the pastor's role as a counsellor of souls equipped by Scripture.

The movement has matured significantly since Adams. Figures like David Powlison, Ed Welch, Paul Tripp, and Winston Smith have developed a richer, more pastorally sensitive approach — one that takes suffering seriously, engages with the complexity of human experience, and refuses to reduce every problem to simple sin patterns. The goal of this study is to equip every Christian — not just pastors — to serve one another in the hard places of life.

Six units: (1) Foundations — why Scripture is sufficient; (2) Understanding People — the biblical anatomy of the soul; (3) Sin, Suffering, and Sanctification — distinguishing and relating them; (4) The Heart — where counseling actually happens; (5) Listening and Speaking — the practice of gospel conversation; (6) Common Struggles — applying biblical counsel to anxiety, depression, anger, and grief.

1.title: Foundations: The Sufficiency of Scripture
1.overview:
Every counseling approach rests on a set of assumptions about what is wrong with human beings and what can make them well. Secular psychology assumes that the fundamental problem is psychological — rooted in developmental history, neurological patterns, or environmental conditioning — and that the solution lies in insight, relearning, or medication. Biblical counseling does not dismiss the reality of these factors, but it insists that the deepest problem is spiritual and moral: the human heart turned away from God, seeking life in things that cannot give it, and bearing the weight of a disordered will.

The foundation of biblical counseling is the sufficiency of Scripture — not Scripture's exhaustiveness (the Bible does not address every question) but its adequacy: it gives us everything we need to understand people and to point them toward genuine flourishing. Peter's statement is breathtaking in its scope: God has granted us everything pertaining to life and godliness through the knowledge of him (2 Pet 1:3). Everything. Not most things. Not the spiritual things, with the psychological things handled elsewhere. Everything that pertains to life — not just church life but the whole texture of human experience.

This does not make the counsellor an expert in neurology or pharmacology — those are genuine domains of medical knowledge. But it does make the counsellor who knows Scripture and knows the human heart equipped to address the soul's deepest needs in a way that no amount of psychological training alone can. The counsellor's greatest tool is not a technique but a text — and behind the text, a Person who knows every counselee better than they know themselves.
1.theology:
Sola Scriptura applied to counseling: The Reformation's insistence on Scripture's supreme authority extends to the care of souls. The church does not need a supplementary psychology to understand or help people — she needs to know her Bible more deeply, apply it more wisely, and deliver it more compassionately. This does not mean ignoring medical knowledge (the doctor treats the body; the counsellor addresses the soul), but it does mean refusing to subordinate biblical categories to psychological ones. Sin is not a disorder. Repentance is not an insight. The new birth is not a cognitive restructuring.

The image of God: People are made in God's image (Gen 1:26–27) — rational, relational, volitional, and worshipful. The Fall has distorted but not destroyed this image. Every human being, however broken, retains the image of God, which means they have genuine dignity, genuine moral agency, and genuine capacity for relationship with God. Biblical counseling treats people as image-bearers, not as cases or diagnostic categories.

The nature of change: Genuine change — the kind that biblical counseling aims at — is not behavioural modification but transformation of the heart by the Spirit through the Word. It looks like increasing conformity to Christ (Rom 8:29), growing love for God and neighbour, decreasing dominion of sinful patterns. It is always partial and incomplete in this life, always dependent on grace, always oriented toward the resurrection.
1.examples:
Jay Adams and the recovery of pastoral counseling: Before Adams, most seminaries trained pastors in preaching and theology but referred psychological problems to secular therapists. Adams's bold claim — that Scripture is sufficient and that pastors can and should counsel from it — was controversial but catalytic. He was not always right in every application, but he was right on the essential point: the church had surrendered a territory she should never have abandoned.

David Powlison's contribution: Powlison refined Adams's approach with greater pastoral sensitivity, a richer understanding of suffering, and a deeper grasp of how the gospel addresses not just guilt but fear, shame, grief, and confusion. His essay "X-ray Questions" — a tool for helping people identify the desires of the heart — became a foundational text for a generation of biblical counselors. He showed that biblical counseling is not a blunt instrument but a scalpel.

verseByVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The sufficiency claim rests here. All things — pertaining to life and godliness — are granted through the knowledge of God. This is not a promise that the Bible will tell you how to rewire a house or perform an appendectomy. It is a promise that in knowing God — through his Word, his Son, his Spirit — the soul has everything it needs to live well and grow holy. The biblical counselor does not come to the counselee with a handful of techniques; she comes with knowledge of the God who made and redeemed this person. That is everything.

verseByVerse.quote: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Notice the four uses of Scripture that Paul names: teaching (telling us what is true), reproof (showing us where we have gone wrong), correction (pointing us back to the right path), and training in righteousness (developing the habits of the godly life). This is a perfect description of what biblical counseling does: it teaches the truth about God and the soul, reproves sinful patterns of thought and action, corrects course through repentance and grace, and trains the counselee in the practices that lead to flourishing. The man — or woman — of God who counsels from Scripture is not impoverished; they are complete, equipped for every good work, including the good work of caring for souls.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The biblical counselor's primary tool is a sword — not a blunt instrument but a precision instrument that cuts to the exact depth required, discerning not just behaviour but motive, not just what the counselee has done but why. No psychological assessment tool, however sophisticated, can do this. The Word of God is living — it is not a static collection of ancient wisdom but the voice of the living God, active in the soul of the counselee even before the counselor speaks. The counselor's task is to bring the sharp edge of this living Word to bear on the specific contours of this specific person's heart.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's word for instruct is nouthetein — the root of Adams's "nouthetic counseling." And Paul addresses it not to a professional guild of trained therapists but to the whole congregation: ordinary Christians, full of goodness and knowledge, able to counsel one another. This is the biblical counseling movement's great democratising conviction: the cure of souls is not a specialist's monopoly but the church's corporate calling. Every mature believer, shaped by the Word, can serve as a counselor to their brother or sister. The pastor equips, trains, and handles the complex cases — but every member of the body is a potential instrument of grace in another's life.

2.title: Understanding People: The Biblical Anatomy of the Soul
2.overview:
Before you can counsel anyone, you need to understand them — not just their presenting problem but who they are as human beings. Biblical counseling begins with a thick account of the person: made in God's image, fallen in Adam, redeemable in Christ, indwelt by the Spirit, living in a body, shaped by a history, embedded in relationships, situated in a world that both blesses and afflicts them.

The secular psychological account of persons tends to be thin in certain ways: it typically cannot account for genuine moral responsibility (if all behaviour is caused by prior factors, who is responsible for anything?), genuine hope (if the deepest self is defined by trauma or neurochemistry, what can change?), or the ultimate good (what is the human being for?). The biblical account is richer: persons are agents who make real choices and bear real moral responsibility; they are beloved image-bearers whose dignity no amount of suffering can extinguish; they are headed for a resurrection that will more than compensate for everything lost in this life.

Biblical counseling uses the category of the heart as its central diagnostic category. The heart in Scripture is not the emotions (as in modern usage) but the entire inner person — the seat of thought, desire, will, and worship. Whatever captures the heart directs the life. Counseling, at its deepest, is the work of helping a person see what has captured their heart and inviting them to give it back to God.
2.theology:
The biblical anatomy: Scripture speaks of the human person in terms of heart, soul, mind, strength, spirit, and body — not as separate compartments but as interlocking dimensions of a unified person. Paul prays for the Thessalonians' spirit, soul, and body to be preserved blameless (1 Thess 5:23). Jesus commands love of God with heart, soul, mind, and strength (Mark 12:30). The counselor works with the whole person — bodily symptoms may have spiritual roots; spiritual distress manifests in the body; relational patterns reveal the heart's allegiances.

Functional theology: What a person actually believes — not what they say they believe but what their behaviour reveals they believe — is their functional theology. A person may confess that God is sovereign and good, and yet live in chronic anxiety as though God cannot be trusted. Biblical counseling helps the counselee identify the gap between their stated theology and their functional theology, and calls them to greater integrity: to live as though what they say is true is actually true.

The flesh and the Spirit: Paul's language of "flesh" (sarx) refers not to the physical body but to the old self — the sin-bent orientation that remains in the believer even after regeneration (Gal 5:16–17). The counselee is not simply a sinner to be reproved; they are a saint in whom the Spirit dwells and the flesh remains. Counseling must address both realities: the genuine newness that the Spirit has created, and the ongoing struggle with the flesh that will not be fully resolved until glory.
2.examples:
Ed Welch on weakness: Ed Welch's Shame Interrupted and Running Scared demonstrate the richness of the biblical account of persons. Rather than diagnosing anxiety as merely sinful distrust, Welch explores the many dimensions of fear — the legitimate fears, the distorted fears, the fears rooted in past wounds, the fears that masquerade as wisdom. His counseling is compassionate precisely because his anthropology is thick: he sees the whole person, not just the presenting symptom.

Paul Tripp on the heart: Paul Tripp's Instruments in the Redeemer's Hands opens with the observation that every human being is always interpreting their experience through a lens of desire — what they love, what they fear, what they are living for. The counselor's first task is not to fix behaviour but to understand the desires that are producing it. This is a deeply Augustinian insight: the will follows the loves. Change the loves, and the life changes.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The heart is the source — not a passive reservoir but the spring from which all of life flows. What enters the heart flows into every word, decision, relationship, and habit. This is why biblical counseling focuses on the heart rather than behaviour: to change behaviour without changing the heart is to dam a river without addressing the spring. The dam breaks eventually. The spring keeps flowing. Counseling that addresses only outward patterns — anger management, communication skills, coping strategies — is treating symptoms. The biblical counselor goes upstream.

verseByVerse.quote: For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus overturns the Pharisaic assumption that sin is primarily an external problem — a matter of what you touch, eat, or encounter. Sin's root is internal: the corrupt heart produces corrupt fruit. This is both humbling (the problem is inside, not in our circumstances) and hopeful (if the heart can be changed, everything can change). The Pharisee was trying to manage the fruit by controlling the environment. Jesus cuts to the root. Biblical counseling follows Jesus: it is not primarily behaviour modification but heart transformation.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's prayer for the whole person — spirit, soul, and body — reflects the biblical refusal to spiritualise away the physical or physicalise away the spiritual. The body matters: chronic pain, illness, and exhaustion affect the soul's capacity for worship and relationship. The soul matters: grief, shame, and anxiety are real and serious, not merely chemical events. The spirit matters: the deepest orientation of the person toward or away from God shapes everything else. Biblical counseling works with all of this, referring to physicians when the body needs treatment and addressing the soul when the soul needs the Word.

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The conflict Paul describes is not between body and soul (Greek dualism) but between the old self and the new — the flesh (the sin-bent nature) and the Spirit (the new creation life). Every believer lives in this tension. The counselee who is struggling with a persistent sin pattern is not failing to become a Christian — they are discovering what it means to be one. The counselor's task is not to shame them for the conflict but to call them to walk by the Spirit — to feed the new nature by means of grace (Word, prayer, community) and starve the flesh by turning away from its occasions.

3.title: Sin, Suffering, and Sanctification
3.overview:
One of the most important skills in biblical counseling is the ability to distinguish between sin and suffering — and then to hold them together in the right relationship. Many counseling failures come from getting this wrong: treating every problem as a sin issue (which crushes suffering people under a weight of guilt they do not deserve) or treating every problem as a suffering issue (which removes responsibility and short-circuits growth).

Sin is the counselee's own moral failure — the ways they have turned from God and harmed themselves and others. Suffering is what has been done to them or what has happened to them — the losses, traumas, injustices, and griefs that no human being deserves or chooses. Both are real, and both are addressed by the gospel.

But the relationship between sin and suffering is complex. Sin produces suffering — both in the sinner (the fruit of sinful choices is always painful) and in others (sin wounds those around the sinner). Suffering can produce sin — the person overwhelmed by grief or pain is tempted toward bitterness, withdrawal, or despair. And suffering can be completely unrelated to personal sin — Job's comforters made this error, and Jesus corrected it explicitly (John 9:3).

Sanctification — the Spirit's work of making believers progressively holy — happens in the middle of this. Neither sin nor suffering defeats it; God uses both as instruments of growth. The counselor's role is to trace how God is at work in this particular person's particular struggle, and to call them to cooperate with that work through faith and repentance.
3.theology:
Distinguishing sin and suffering: The practical skill requires theological clarity. Not every struggle is a sin to be repented of; some struggles are a suffering to be lamented, endured, and brought to God in prayer. A person grieving the loss of a child does not need to be told what sin is making them grieve — they need Job's friends to sit with them in the dust. A person in a persistent angry pattern does need to be shown the sinful desire beneath the anger. The counselor must listen carefully to distinguish which is which — and most complex situations involve both.

Suffering as gift: James 1:2–4 and Romans 5:3–5 both present suffering as an occasion for joy — not because pain is pleasant but because God uses trials to produce tested character, endurance, and hope. This is not a glib reassurance ("everything happens for a reason") but a theological conviction: the God who governs all things is at work in even the worst suffering, conforming his children to Christ. The counselor can say this only from within genuine empathy with the counselee's pain — said too quickly, it is a theological bludgeon.

Repentance: Repentance is not merely behavioural change — it is a change of mind (metanoia) about God, self, and the world, leading to a changed direction of life. It involves seeing one's sin as God sees it (grievous, deserving judgment), fleeing to Christ (who bore that judgment), and turning toward new patterns of thought and action. It is not a one-time crisis event but a daily posture — the Christian life is, as Luther said, one of continual repentance.
3.examples:
Welch on suffering vs. sin: Ed Welch tells the story of a counselee who had been abused as a child and was struggling with deep shame and distorted thinking about God. A less careful counselor might have focused on the counselee's sinful responses (bitterness, distorted beliefs). Welch began with the suffering — sitting with the pain, lamenting the injustice, assuring the counselee of God's compassion. Only from that foundation — once trust was established and the suffering was truly heard — could repentance conversations begin about the counselee's own responses.

Tripp on marriage counseling: Paul Tripp observes that couples in conflict almost always come with a detailed catalogue of the other person's sins and a very short list of their own. The counselor's first task is to help each partner see their own contribution to the dynamic — not to deny the other's failures but to locate the one place they can actually do something: their own heart. This requires the security of the gospel: the person who knows they are fully loved and fully forgiven by God can bear to see their own sin clearly, because they know seeing it does not destroy them.

verseByVerse.quote: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James does not say feel joy — he says count it joy, which is an act of the mind, a choice of interpretation. The trial is real and painful; the joy is not denial but reframing through faith. You know something about this trial that changes everything: it is doing something. The testing of faith produces steadfastness — the root verb (hupomone) means remaining under pressure rather than escaping it. The counselee who endures the trial rather than fleeing it is being formed. That formation is God's gift, and the counselor's task is to help the counselee see it.

verseByVerse.quote: We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's chain — suffering → endurance → character → hope — is not automatic. It describes the trajectory of suffering that is processed with God, through faith, in the community of the church. Suffering that is denied, avoided, or endured alone does not produce character; it produces bitterness, numbness, or despair. The difference is the Spirit: God's love is poured into the heart by the Spirit, and it is that love — experienced, not merely believed abstractly — that transforms suffering into growth. The biblical counselor is an instrument of that Spirit-mediated love.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples' question reflects a common pastoral error: assuming that suffering is always the direct consequence of specific sin. Jesus corrects it without qualification — this man's blindness was not caused by his sin or his parents' sin. Sometimes suffering is simply suffering: the brokenness of a fallen world experienced by a specific person for God's purposes, which are larger than any simple retributive calculus. The counselor who too quickly looks for the sin behind the suffering will wound those who are suffering innocently — and there are many. Job's comforters were wrong. Jesus is the better counselor.

verseByVerse.quote: For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul distinguishes two kinds of sorrow. Godly grief leads somewhere: to repentance, to freedom, to life. It faces the sin honestly, feels its weight, and moves toward God with it. Worldly grief — what we might call guilt without grace — circles endlessly: it feels the weight but finds no relief, because it is directed toward self (self-condemnation, self-punishment) rather than toward God (who forgives). The biblical counselor's task is to help the counselee move from worldly grief — which is real and often intense — to godly grief that resolves in the grace of the gospel. The resolution is not cheap — it costs Christ everything. But it is real, and it is complete.

4.title: The Heart: Where Counseling Actually Happens
4.overview:
Biblical counseling's central diagnostic category is the heart. In Scripture, the heart is not primarily the seat of emotion (as in modern usage) but the inner person — the place of thought, desire, will, and worship. It is the control centre of the human being, the source from which all behaviour flows. Every presenting problem in counseling — every conflict, addiction, anxiety, depression, and relational breakdown — has a heart dimension that underlies and drives it.

The heart's fundamental orientation is worshipful: human beings are always organised around something, always deriving their identity and security from something, always living for something. Augustine famously said that the human heart is restless until it finds its rest in God. The Fall has not changed the heart's structure (it is still worshipful) but has redirected its worship: the fallen heart worships created things rather than the Creator. It finds its security in approval, control, comfort, achievement, or relationships rather than in God — and these misplaced loves are the root of most of the presenting problems that biblical counseling addresses.

Paul Tripp's X-ray questions are diagnostic tools for revealing these hidden heart allegiances: What do you love most in this situation? What would be a catastrophe for you? What would make you feel safe? What are you most afraid of? What do you feel you deserve? These questions are not techniques — they are ways of helping the counselee see their own heart with the kind of clarity that only God's Word can provide.
4.theology:
Idolatry as the root issue: Tim Keller (following Tripp and Powlison, who follow Calvin's Institutes) identifies idolatry — the worship of created things in place of God — as the root beneath most presenting problems. The angry person is typically worshipping something (control, justice, approval) that is being threatened. The anxious person is typically worshipping something (safety, comfort, reputation) that feels at risk. The depressed person may have lost something (a relationship, an achievement, an identity) that had become a functional god. The counselor helps the counselee identify the idol and call them to repentance — not just for the symptom but for the misplaced love beneath it.

Desires and their disorder: Desires are not intrinsically sinful — God made human beings to desire. The problem is when good desires (for love, security, justice, comfort) become ruling desires — when they cross the line from "I want this" to "I must have this or my life is over." James 4:1–2 traces conflict to desires that war within us — the Greek word is hedonon (pleasures/desires). The counselor's task is not to eliminate desire but to reorder it: to help the counselee desire God above everything, so that lesser desires find their right place.

The gospel as the answer: The heart's misplaced loves cannot be corrected by willpower, insight, or behavioural change — they require the gospel. The person who knows that God's love is unconditional, that their identity is secure in Christ, that their ultimate safety is guaranteed by the resurrection — that person is freed from the anxious grasping of idolatry. The gospel does not merely forgive the sins produced by idolatry; it addresses the idolatry itself by giving the heart something better to love.
4.examples:
Keller on counterfeit gods: Tim Keller's Counterfeit Gods applies the idol-diagnosis to the most common allegiances: money, sex, power, and approval. His chapter on the idol of approval — the desperate need to be liked and validated — names a struggle that is almost universal in contemporary culture. The person who cannot bear criticism, who shapes every relationship around the question "Do they like me?", who collapses at rejection — this person is not merely emotionally fragile; they are looking to human approval for something only God can give. The counselor who names this gently and clearly, and then points to the God whose approval is given freely in Christ, has done something genuinely therapeutic.

Tripp on marriage: Tripp's What Did You Expect? applies heart-level diagnosis to marriage. Most marital conflict, he argues, is not really about the dishes or the schedule or the in-laws — it is about two people each demanding from the marriage something only God can provide: unconditional love, perfect understanding, complete security. Marriage cannot bear that weight. No human being can. When the counselor helps a couple see that they are asking from each other what only God gives, it does not minimise the real grievances — but it changes the emotional temperature and opens a path toward genuine forgiveness and realistic love.

verseByVerse.quote: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James diagnoses conflict at the deepest level: it originates not in the other person's behaviour but in the desires warring within. The quarrelling person thinks the problem is what the other person did or failed to do — James says the problem is inside. There is a desire that is not being met, and the unmet desire is producing anger, manipulation, and conflict. This is not a comfortable diagnosis. But it is a hopeful one: if the root is in my heart, I can do something about it. I cannot change the other person, but by God's grace I can bring my warring desires to God and find in him what I was wrongly demanding from the other.

verseByVerse.quote: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Treasure reveals heart — not the reverse. Jesus does not say "where your heart is, your treasure will follow" but the opposite: the thing you pour your resources, attention, and energy into is the thing that owns your heart. The counselor who wants to understand the counselee's heart asks not "What do you feel?" but "What do you pour yourself into? What do you sacrifice for? What do you daydream about? What would you do anything to protect?" The answers reveal the treasure, and the treasure reveals the heart. And the heart is where counseling happens.

verseByVerse.quote: For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence; from him comes my salvation. He only is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Psalmist is preaching to himself — commanding his own soul to wait on God alone. This is the alternative to idolatry: not the suppression of desire but the redirection of it. God alone — not God plus approval, not God plus security, not God plus success. He only is the rock; everything else shifts. The counselee who has discovered this — not merely as a doctrine but as a lived reality — has found the foundation that cannot be shaken. The counselor's deepest aim is to help the counselee get here: to the place where God alone is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The most important thing the counselor must know is that heart change is God's work, not theirs. The counselor speaks, listens, questions, encourages, and rebukes — but only God can remove the heart of stone and give the heart of flesh. This is the theological foundation of counseling humility: the counselor is not the agent of change but the instrument. The Surgeon operates; the counselor hands the instruments. This prevents both despair (when people don't change quickly) and pride (when they do). God gives new hearts. We tell people about the God who gives them.

5.title: Listening and Speaking: The Practice of Gospel Conversation
5.overview:
Biblical counseling is a conversation — a particular kind of conversation, conducted with prayer, shaped by Scripture, and aimed at the transformation of the counselee by the grace of God. Learning to have this conversation is a skill that can be developed, and this unit explores the two fundamental dimensions of that skill: listening and speaking.

Most Christians are poor listeners — not because they are unkind but because they are too quick to speak. They hear the problem and immediately reach for a solution, a verse, or a story from their own experience. This well-intentioned helpfulness often leaves the counselee feeling unheard and the counselor misinformed about what is really happening. Proverbs 18:13 is severe about this: "If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame." The counselor who speaks before truly listening has identified the wrong problem and applied the wrong solution.

Good listening requires more than patience — it requires a genuine desire to understand the counselee's experience from the inside. It means asking questions that draw out rather than questions that merely confirm what the counselor already thinks. It means attending to what is not said as much as to what is said: the topic avoided, the emotion that briefly surfaced and was quickly suppressed, the answer that was technically true but felt rehearsed.

Gospel speaking — once the counselor has truly heard — means speaking truth that is both accurate and kind, that addresses the heart not just the behaviour, that is soaked in grace even when it is direct. It means knowing when to comfort and when to challenge, when to wait and when to speak, when to name sin and when simply to sit in sorrow. It is an art, and it is learned only by practice under the Spirit's guidance.
5.theology:
The ministry of presence: Before you speak, you sit. Job's friends, for all their subsequent failures, did one right thing first: they sat with him in silence for seven days (Job 2:13). There is a ministry in simply being present with suffering — not fixing, not explaining, not theologising, just being there. This is what the incarnation models: God did not address human suffering from a distance. He entered it. The counselor who has truly entered the counselee's world — who has heard, understood, and felt the weight of it — is in a position to speak. The counselor who has not cannot.

Nouthetic instruction: The biblical model of counseling involves instruction (teaching what is true), admonition (warning about dangerous patterns), and encouragement (urging toward the good). Paul describes his ministry in Colossians 1:28: "warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom." Warning and teaching — not one or the other but both, in the right proportion for each person in each situation. The counselor who only warns produces guilt; the counselor who only teaches produces knowledge without change. Wisdom knows which is needed when.

Speaking the truth in love: Ephesians 4:15 gives the two-dimensional standard: truth and love. Truth without love is cruelty; love without truth is sentimentality. The counselor who speaks truth — about sin, about the gospel, about what God requires — and speaks it in love, with genuine care for the counselee's flourishing, is doing something profoundly Christlike. Christ spoke the most searching truth ever spoken and was the most loving person who ever lived. His example does not make truth-speaking comfortable, but it does make it possible.
5.examples:
Paul Tripp on entering the story: Tripp's model of counseling begins with what he calls "entering the person's story" — taking time to understand their history, their relationships, their losses, and their joys before making any diagnosis. This is not merely a rapport-building technique; it is a theological conviction that this person's experience matters and that the counselor who skips it will miss what God is doing in this person's specific life. God's grace is always particular — it reaches this person in this situation. The counselor must know the situation to trace the grace.

Winston Smith on tone: Winston Smith of the Christian Counseling and Educational Foundation (CCEF) has written compellingly about the tone of gospel conversations. The counselee who is already crushed by shame or grief does not need a counselor who adds to the weight. They need someone who speaks with the tone of Jesus to the woman caught in adultery: "Neither do I condemn you — go, and from now on sin no more" (John 8:11). The grace comes first. The call to change comes from within the grace, not before it.

verseByVerse.quote: If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most practically important verses for counselors. The temptation to answer before truly hearing is almost universal — we hear a problem that resembles one we have encountered before, and we reach for the solution that worked there. But every person is particular; every situation has dimensions that only careful listening will reveal. The counselor who has not truly heard has not truly understood, and the answer they give — however correct in the abstract — will land in the wrong place. Listening is not a preliminary courtesy before the real work begins; it is the beginning of the real work.

verseByVerse.quote: Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's counseling model is Christ-centred (him we proclaim), comprehensive (everyone), and dual-directional (warning and teaching). The goal is not resolved presenting problems but maturity in Christ — a person who knows Christ more deeply, loves him more fully, and lives more consistently with that love. This is the long-game of biblical counseling: not merely symptom relief but Christlikeness. The counselor who keeps this goal in view will not be satisfied with a counselee who feels better if they do not yet know Christ better. Feeling better is a mercy; knowing Christ is the goal.

verseByVerse.quote: Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The two-dimensional standard. Truth without love becomes a weapon — accurate, precise, and wounding without healing. Love without truth becomes a deception — comfortable, affirming, and ultimately useless. The counselor who loves the counselee enough to tell them the truth — and who tells them the truth from within genuine love — is doing something rare and precious. It is not easy to hold both together; the temptation is always to slide into one or the other. The counselor who prays for wisdom to speak truthfully and lovingly is asking for a grace that only God can supply.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Job's friends' finest hour — before they opened their mouths. Seven days of silent, present solidarity with a man in catastrophic suffering. They did not explain, minimise, or theologise. They simply sat with him. This is the ministry of presence, and it is often the most important thing a counselor can do in the early stages of caring for someone in acute grief. The time for speaking comes — and when it comes, Job's friends proved disastrously wrong. But their initial posture was right: the suffering person needs to be accompanied before they need to be instructed. Go and sit before you speak.

6.title: Common Struggles: Anxiety, Depression, Anger, and Grief
6.overview:
This final unit applies the principles of the previous five to the four most common struggles that bring people to counseling. Anxiety. Depression. Anger. Grief. These are not rare conditions for the especially troubled — they are the ordinary afflictions of ordinary human beings living in a broken world. Every congregation contains people wrestling with all four, often in combination, often in silence.

Biblical counseling does not claim to have simple answers to complex conditions. Anxiety has biological, situational, relational, and spiritual dimensions; so does depression. Anger can be righteous or sinful; so can grief have godly and ungodly expressions. The counselor who approaches these struggles with a single solution — "just trust God more" — will cause harm. The counselor who approaches them with genuine curiosity, careful listening, theological depth, and gospel confidence will be an instrument of grace.

Two notes on medical questions: (1) For severe depression or anxiety with physiological components, collaboration with a physician is appropriate and wise — the body and soul are not separate, and sometimes the body needs treatment that counseling alone cannot provide. (2) Medication does not replace the need for heart-level work — it may create the conditions in which that work becomes possible. The biblical counselor refers when referral is appropriate, collaborates when collaboration is possible, and always continues to address the soul.
6.theology:
Anxiety: At its root, anxiety is a failure of trust — not primarily a character flaw but a spiritual wound. The anxious person is trying to hold their world together by the force of their own vigilance, because they have not yet found it safe to release it into God's hands. Jesus' repeated command — "Do not be anxious" — is not a rebuke but a call: you do not need to carry this. The cure for anxiety is not relaxation techniques but a bigger view of God: his sovereignty, his goodness, his knowledge of our situation, his proven faithfulness. The counselor who can bring this big view of God to the anxious person — slowly, patiently, with genuine compassion — is doing the most therapeutic thing possible.

Depression: Depression is complex — it has biological, situational, and spiritual dimensions that often cannot be neatly separated. Biblically, we see depression in Elijah (1 Kgs 19), the Psalmist (Ps 88), Jeremiah (Jer 20), and Paul (2 Cor 1:8). God does not rebuke these sufferers — he meets them with physical provision (Elijah), honest lament (the Psalms), and the comfort of resurrection hope (2 Corinthians). The depressed person may need to be urged back to the means of grace; they may need to have the darkness named and lamented; they may need to be helped to see that their depressed thoughts are lying to them about God, themselves, and the future.

Anger: Anger is not intrinsically sinful — God is angry at injustice (Ps 7:11), and Jesus drove money-changers from the temple (John 2:15–17). But human anger is almost always mixed: righteous anger at genuine wrong mixed with self-righteous anger at wounded pride. The counselor helps the angry person ask: What was threatened? Was it genuinely worth defending? Am I responding proportionately? What do I want to happen — justice, or punishment? James 1:19–20 gives the rule: slow to anger, because human anger does not produce God's righteousness.

Grief: Grief is not a problem to be solved but an experience to be accompanied. The Bible does not call us to avoid grief — Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35) even knowing he was about to raise him. The biblical framework for grief is lament: honest, raw, God-directed expressions of pain, loss, and bewilderment. The Psalms are forty percent lament — God has given his people a language for grief. The grieving counselee does not need to be moved quickly to acceptance; they need to be helped to grieve honestly, toward God, trusting that he receives the lament and holds the sufferer.
6.examples:
Elijah and the angel: 1 Kings 19 is the Bible's most detailed account of what we might call burnout and depression. Elijah, after the greatest victory of his prophetic ministry, collapses under a juniper tree and asks to die. God's response is remarkable: he does not rebuke, lecture, or even pray with Elijah. He feeds him. Twice. "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you." Physical provision before spiritual instruction. The body's needs are real and must be addressed before the soul's counsel can be received. This is a model for pastoral care of the exhausted and depressed.

The Psalms of lament: Psalms 22, 42, 43, 88, and 139 give the grieving and depressed a language they often cannot find on their own. Psalm 88 ends with no resolution — only darkness. It is the one psalm that does not turn the corner into praise. Its presence in the canon is a gift: God is not frightened by honest, unresolved lament. The counselor who gives the grieving person the psalms of lament is giving them both permission to grieve and a companion for the journey.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The structure is precise: the alternative to anxiety is not resolution of the problem but prayer. Paul does not say "do not be anxious because everything will work out" — he says bring your anxiety to God in prayer with thanksgiving, and the peace of God (which does not depend on circumstances) will stand guard over your heart. The anxious person does not need their circumstances to change first; they need to pray. The guard comes after the prayer, not after the situation resolves. This is simultaneously profoundly simple and profoundly difficult — and the counselor who helps the anxious person actually pray (not just be told to pray) is helping them access the only cure anxiety has.

verseByVerse.quote: And he lay down and slept under a juniper tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, "Arise and eat." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's first response to Elijah's suicidal depression is not a sermon but a meal. He lets the exhausted prophet sleep and then feeds him — twice. This is not a failure of spiritual care; it is a model of it. The person in acute distress needs their basic needs met before they can receive counsel. The counselor who insists on heart-level spiritual conversation with someone who has not slept in three days or has not eaten is not being spiritually serious — they are being pastorally unwise. Arise and eat. Then we will talk about the journey.

verseByVerse.quote: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The rule for anger is the rhythm of the counseling relationship itself: quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. Most of the damage done in anger is done by people who inverted this sequence: quick to anger, quick to speak, and — if they are honest — slow to hear. Human anger (the anger that flows from wounded pride, frustrated desire, or threatened control) does not produce God's righteousness — it produces further damage. The counselor helps the angry person slow down: What did you actually hear? What were you feeling before the anger? What did you want? What did you fear? Slowing the sequence down creates space for the Spirit to interrupt it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus wept. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The shortest verse in the Bible and one of the most theologically weighty. Jesus knew he was about to raise Lazarus. He knew the story ended well. He wept anyway — because Mary was weeping, because death is an enemy, because grief is real and he refused to hold himself above it. This is the incarnation at its most intimate: God entering human grief not as a visitor who remains above it but as a participant who feels it. The counselor who has learned to weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15) — not performing empathy but genuinely entering the suffering of the counselee — is reflecting something of Christ. Grief does not need to be fixed immediately. It needs to be accompanied. Jesus shows us how.
